extracted.intended_audience: judges, law clerks, administrative-law scholars, practitioners, and law students interested in APA rulemaking and judicial review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative framework for judicial review of agency 'good cause' determinations under the Administrative Procedure Act, including the appropriate standard of review and the interests courts should balance when agencies bypass notice-and-comment rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause exception — intended narrow use
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA’s drafters intended that [the good cause] exception to be reserved for rare instances when exigency outweighed strong interests in public participation and agency deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the exception only in genuinely exigent circumstances where waiting for notice-and-comment would frustrate an important regulatory objective; treat routine or predictable situations skeptically. The historical/legislative purpose supports a narrow construction that privileges public participation and agency deliberation except in urgent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess agency invocation frequency and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies currently claim good cause to skip notice-and-comment requirements in a significant percentage of rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the pattern and frequency of an agency's good-cause invocations as evidence of potential misuse. A high volume of invocations is an anti-pattern suggesting the exception is being treated as routine rather than exceptional, warranting closer judicial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review — de novo review of agency assertions of good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should review agency assertions of good cause de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note argues that the APA’s text, structure, and objectives, together with principles of administrative deference, mandate de novo review for good-cause claims. De novo review requires courts to independently determine whether the statutory criteria for bypassing notice-and-comment are met, rather than deferring to the agency's characterization of facts or urgency. This standard is proposed as the best way to address inter-circuit divergence and to ensure agencies do not evade procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing the competing interests when evaluating good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments of good cause should properly balance the competing interests of public participation, agency flexibility, public safety, and judicial administrability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether good cause exists, courts should weigh: (1) the public’s interest in notice-and-comment and informed deliberation; (2) agencies’ need for flexibility to act quickly when truly necessary; (3) the importance of protecting public health, safety, or other urgent interests; and (4) practical limits on courts’ ability to administer highly deferential or fact-intensive reviews. The chosen standard should strike an appropriate balance among these considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer judicial solutions over statutory amendment for correcting misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Amending the good-cause exception is characterized as unrealistic and undesirable; courts are best situated to ensure proper use of the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legislative amendment is unlikely or undesirable, courts should adopt and apply robust interpretive standards (e.g., de novo review) to police agency use of the exception. This emphasizes shaping doctrine through judicial interpretation rather than relying on Congress to revise the statute.
